slides.teaching: Preview that today's four steps are the same four steps as Meeting A's closing process slide, just run for real.

slides.title: Recall five terms from Meeting A
rows: a DataFrame with a geometry column and a CRS
what a coordinate means; a numeric ID for it
convert coordinates to a different CRS
attribute join on a shared column value
join zone_summary onto zones by zone
a map shaded by an attribute value
shade each zone by mean energy
slides.callout: Every term above appears at least once in today's script - point to it as you reach that line.
slides.teaching: Adapted from the Week 3B recall-table pattern. Ask students to find each term already in the printed handout before running cell [1].

slides.title: Today's pipeline is four ordered steps

steps.label: SUMMARIZE
steps.head: Recall Week 5
steps.body: Group building_rooms.csv by zone - mean energy, mean area, room count.

steps.label: MERGE
steps.head: Attribute join
steps.body: zones.merge(zone_summary, on='zone') attaches those numbers to each polygon.

steps.label: REPROJECT
steps.head: to_crs()
steps.body: Convert from EPSG:4326 (degrees) to EPSG:32618, UTM 18N (meters), before measuring.

steps.label: MAP
steps.head: Compute + plot
steps.body: footprint area, then one static choropleth colored by mean energy.

slides.teaching: This slide is the map of the whole studio - refer back to it before each new cell.

slides.title: [1] Recall Week 5: one row of attributes per zone
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

rooms = pd.read_csv('building_rooms.csv')
zone_summary = rooms.groupby('zone').agg(
    mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr=('energy_kwh_m2_yr', 'mean'),
    mean_area_m2=('area_m2', 'mean'),
    room_count=('room_id', 'count'),
).reset_index()
print(zone_summary)
slides.output:
zone  mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr  mean_area_m2  room_count
0  North              64.250000        40.975          12
1  South             115.681818        38.250          12
slides.explainHead: Same finding as Week 5, no new numbers
slides.explainBody: This is the exact groupby from Week 5, just with renamed, unit-labeled columns so they merge cleanly onto geometry later. Two rows, one per zone - South still runs roughly 80% higher energy use intensity than North, the same finding you have already seen twice.
slides.teaching: Ask students to predict which zone will be higher before running - by now they should say South from memory.

slides.title: Studio 1: verify the recalled summary matches Week 5
slides.prompt: Before moving on, confirm this table has not silently changed.
steps: Predict mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr for both zones from memory.
Run the cell and compare.
Check room_count sums to 24 across both zones.
Note this is attribute data only - no geometry yet.
slides.teaching: This step matters precisely because Meeting B is about to attach these numbers to shapes - any silent drift here would poison the map.

slides.title: [2] Load the zone geometry and inspect its CRS
slides.code:
import geopandas as gpd

zones = gpd.read_file('zone_footprints.geojson')
print(zones)
print('CRS:', zones.crs)
slides.explainBody: Two Radley Hall zone footprints - by construction, each a 24 m x 10 m rectangle (240 m2). The file's CRS is EPSG:4326: longitude/latitude degrees, correct for storage, wrong for measuring - exactly the pitfall named all through Meeting A.
slides.teaching: Have students say the CRS out loud and state, before the next cell, whether it is safe to compute .area right now.

slides.title: [3] Merge the zone summary onto the geometry
slides.code:
zones_merged = zones.merge(zone_summary, on='zone', how='left')
print(type(zones_merged).__name__)
print(zones_merged[['zone', 'mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr', 'mean_area_m2', 'room_count']])
slides.output:
GeoDataFrame
    zone  mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr  mean_area_m2  room_count
0  North              64.250000        40.975          12
1  South             115.681818        38.250          12
slides.explainHead: An ordinary pandas merge, on a GeoDataFrame
slides.explainBody: merge() works exactly as in Week 5 - matching rows by the shared zone column. Because the left side (zones) was a GeoDataFrame, the result stays a GeoDataFrame; the geometry column survives the merge untouched, just with three new attribute columns attached.
slides.teaching: Ask what would happen if one side's zone values were 'north' (lowercase) - preview of the AI-audit bug coming later this studio. Walk through the call left to right on the board: zones (left, keeps geometry), zone_summary (right, attributes only), on='zone' (the shared key).

slides.title: This merge matches by a shared key, not by location
slides.definition: An attribute join (what merge() does) matches rows by comparing values in a shared column - here, zone. It never looks at geometry. A spatial join (gpd.sjoin(), Meeting A) instead matches rows by where their geometries sit in space.

example.head: zones.merge(zone_summary, on='zone', how='left')
example.body: Both tables already share one zone value per row, so a plain attribute join is enough - no geometry comparison needed. gpd.sjoin() is for the opposite case: rows with no shared column, only shared space.

slides.note: merge() runs identically on a plain DataFrame or a GeoDataFrame - it only compares the join column, so a mismatched key (case, spelling) returns NaN, not an error.
slides.teaching: Tie back to 07A's spatial-join process slide and the merge just shown. This is why today's pipeline is a merge, not gpd.sjoin() - Meeting A's spatial join answers a different kind of question.

slides.title: Studio 2: confirm the merge attached the right numbers to the right shape
slides.prompt: A merge can silently attach the wrong row if a key does not match exactly.
steps: Confirm zones_merged still has a geometry column (check .dtypes).
Confirm North's row shows 64.25, South's shows 115.68.
Confirm type(zones_merged) is still a GeoDataFrame, not a plain DataFrame.
State in one sentence why zone must match exactly (case, spelling) on both sides.
slides.teaching: This predicts the AI-audit bug later in the studio - a lowercased key silently drops every match.

slides.title: CRS-choice justification, stated once and reused

left.head: The choice
left.body: EPSG:32618 - UTM zone 18N. Syracuse, NY's longitude (about 76 degrees W) falls inside UTM 18N's 78W-72W band, so this is the correct projected CRS for measuring distance or area here.

right.head: Why write it down
right.body: If you choose the map as your Project 1 Part IV evidence extension (the alternative to Week 6's .gif), it requires a CRS-choice justification note. One sentence, written once, stating the EPSG code and the reason, satisfies that requirement - do this now while the reasoning is fresh.

slides.teaching: Have students write this exact sentence into their own handout before the next cell - it is graded as part of the reproducibility rubric line.

slides.title: Merging attributes does not reproject anything
slides.question: Before reprojecting, what does this print for North?
slides.why: merge() never reprojects. zones_merged stays EPSG:4326, so .area returns square degrees: 2.65e-08 - a warning, not an error.
slides.teaching: Almost everyone predicts a sensible m2 number out of habit. Let the warning print, then read its text aloud before revealing the strip.

slides.title: [4] The pitfall, shown once more, on your own merged data
slides.code:
wrong_area = zones_merged.geometry.area
print('wrong (EPSG:4326) area, North:', f'{wrong_area.iloc[0]:.2e}')
slides.explainBody: zones_merged has not been reprojected yet, so .area still returns square degrees - 2.65e-08, the same tiny, meaningless number from Meeting A's DEMO 2. This also raises a real UserWarning ('Geometry is in a geographic CRS...'), printed to the console, not shown in the output panel here. Notice .area has no parentheses - it is a property you read, not a method you call, unlike .merge() or .to_crs().
slides.teaching: Do not let students skip actually seeing the raw UserWarning print live in the console - read its text aloud before moving on. Also ask why .area has no parentheses, contrasting it with .merge() and .to_crs(), which are both called with ().

slides.title: to_crs() moves coordinates - it does not just relabel them
slides.question: After reprojecting, what does this print for North?
slides.why: to_crs() moves every coordinate to UTM 18N meters, unlike set_crs(); area now measures 239.74 m2, real distortion, not a bug.
slides.teaching: Option C is the set_crs()/to_crs() mixup from 07A - name it explicitly if anyone picks it. Option D reads the wrong column entirely.

slides.title: [5] Reproject, then compute the real spatial metric
slides.explainBody: Both zones are 24 m x 10 m rectangles by construction - 240 m2 exactly. Reprojected and measured correctly, both compute to 239.74 m2: within about 0.1% of ground truth. This is real, small projection distortion, not a mistake - and it is the exact number from Meeting A's DEMO 2, now reproduced on your own merged GeoDataFrame.
slides.teaching: Have students compute the percent difference themselves: (239.74-240)/240*100 = about -0.11%. Small, honest, and worth naming in their own written note.

slides.title: to_crs() returns a brand-new, reprojected GeoDataFrame

parts.label: A new name
parts.body: zones_merged itself is left untouched, still EPSG:4326.

parts.label: Unprojected
parts.body: The GeoDataFrame being converted - read, not modified.

parts.label: Recomputes coordinates
parts.body: Unlike set_crs(), this actually moves every point.

parts.label: Target CRS
parts.body: UTM zone 18N, meters - the correct choice for Syracuse, NY.

slides.teaching: Contrast the chip for zones_utm against the chip for zones_merged - same data, two different names, two different CRSs.

slides.title: Studio 3: check your spatial metric against ground truth
slides.prompt: A measured value with no known truth to compare against cannot be trusted blindly.
steps: State the known ground truth (240 m2) before printing anything.
Run cell [5] and compare footprint_area_m2 to 240.
Compute the percent difference for both zones.
Write one sentence: is this distortion small enough to trust for this map?
slides.teaching: Expected: about 0.11% difference, both zones. Accept 'yes, trustworthy for a zone-level comparison' as the correct judgment, with the percent stated.

slides.title: A choropleth turns one attribute column into map color
slides.definition: A choropleth map shades each polygon by the value of one attribute column - here, mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr. Color encodes a number; the polygon boundary stays the actual geography.

example.head: zones_utm.plot(column='mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr', ...)
example.body: A projected CRS (so shapes are not distorted), a labeled color scale (legend), axis labels stating the CRS and units, and a title - the same fig/ax labeling discipline from Week 6, just applied to a map instead of a scatter plot.

slides.teaching: Connect directly to Week 6's fig/ax/labeled-axes standard - a map is still a Matplotlib figure with the same labeling requirements.

slides.title: Color on a choropleth encodes the value, not the row order
slides.question: Which zone renders visibly darker on the map?
options: North - listed first in the table
South - its mean energy is higher
Neither - plot() needs categories, not numbers
slides.why: column=... shades by that column's own value, numbers included. South nearly doubles North, so OrRd renders it visibly darker.
slides.teaching: Have students name the two numbers the color scale spans before the next slide reveals the actual map.

slides.title: [6] Build the static, labeled choropleth
slides.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
zones_utm.plot(
    column='mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr', cmap='OrRd',
    edgecolor='black', legend=True,
    legend_kwds={'label':
        'Mean energy use intensity (kWh/m2/yr)'},
    ax=ax,
)
ax.set_title('Radley Hall (fictional): EUI by zone')
ax.set_xlabel('Easting (m, EPSG:32618)')
ax.set_ylabel('Northing (m, EPSG:32618)')
fig.savefig('radley_hall_energy_choropleth.png', dpi=150)
slides.explainHead: One line of GeoDataFrame plotting, fully labeled
slides.explainBody: gdf.plot(column=...) is GeoPandas's one-line choropleth: it shades each polygon by that column's value using the cmap color scale. legend=True adds the color-scale key; legend_kwds gives that key its units label - without it the bar has no caption, and a scale with no units is not evidence. South renders visibly darker than North. This call produces a figure, not text, so inspect the saved PNG in Spyder's Plots pane.
slides.teaching: Per course policy, no fabricated text output for a plotting call - describe the figure precisely instead. Confirm this exact code runs cleanly against real geopandas/matplotlib before class.

slides.title: Studio 4: read the map you just made
slides.prompt: A map is only useful if you can say what it shows in one sentence.
steps: Name which zone is visibly darker and why.
State the two numbers the color scale represents (min/max energy).
Confirm axis labels state both units and CRS.
Write the one-sentence design implication this map supports.
slides.teaching: Expected implication, echoing Week 5/6: south-facing exposure plausibly drives higher cooling/solar loads - bounded, not overclaimed, language required.

slides.title: The map this studio produces
slides.alt: Choropleth of the two zone polygons shaded by mean energy use intensity, South visibly darker than North, with a labelled colour bar and axes in meters with the EPSG code.
slides.caption: The deliverable: shaded by mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr, axes in meters, CRS stated, colour bar labelled with its units.
slides.explainHead: Week 5's number, now in a place
slides.explainBody: South renders visibly darker than North. This is the same roughly 80% higher energy finding from Week 5's groupby - but a table cannot show that the difference has a location and an orientation. The labels are not decoration: a map without units and a stated CRS is not reproducible evidence.
slides.teaching: Ask what this map still cannot tell you - occupancy, construction quality, or whether the two zones are even comparable programmes. A choropleth invites over-reading, so name its limits out loud.

slides.title: [6b] By floor, not just by zone: three in-code polygons
slides.explainHead: A GeoDataFrame you build, not one you download
slides.explainBody: rect() writes each floor's footprint as a shapely Polygon literal - the exact pattern CONTRACT.md recommends instead of a live download. All three are built the same size (24m x 10m) as zones_merged, using rooms' own "floor" column (1, 2, 3) as the new join key.
slides.teaching: Point out floors is a GeoDataFrame of exactly three rows, built entirely from numbers typed into this cell - no file, no internet connection, the same technique that authored zone_footprints.geojson in the first place.

slides.title: ...continued: groupby, reproject, merge, measure
slides.code:
floor_summary = rooms.groupby('floor', as_index=False).agg(
    mean_energy=('energy_kwh_m2_yr', 'mean'))
floors_utm = floors.to_crs(32618)
floors_utm['footprint_area_m2'] = floors_utm.area
floors_merged = floors_utm.merge(floor_summary, on='floor')
slides.explainBody: Mean energy rises by floor. Each projected footprint is near the known 240 m² area; small differences are expected projection distortion and should be acknowledged, not hidden.
slides.teaching: Ask why the footprints are close to—but not exactly—240 m². Connect the answer to CRS choice.

slides.title: A mismatched join key fails silently, not with an error
slides.code:
left = pd.DataFrame({'zone': ['North', 'South']})
right = pd.DataFrame({'zone': ['north', 'south'], 'value': [1, 2]})
merged = left.merge(right, on='zone', how='left')
print(merged['value'])
slides.question: What does merged['value'] print?
slides.why: merge() compares strings exactly: North != north, so nothing matches. how=left keeps both rows anyway, just NaN - not an error.
slides.teaching: Option D is true only for how='inner' - name that contrast explicitly. The next slide is exactly this bug, hidden inside a function.

slides.title: [7] AI-audit: two bugs, one merged result
slides.code:
def ai_zone_area_report(rooms_df, zones_gdf):
    zone_summary = rooms_df.groupby('zone').agg(
        mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr=('energy_kwh_m2_yr', 'mean')
    ).reset_index()
    z = zone_summary['zone']
    zone_summary['zone'] = z.str.lower()
    merged = zones_gdf.merge(
        zone_summary, on='zone', how='left')
    merged['area_m2'] = merged.geometry.area
    cols = ['zone', 'area_m2', 'mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr']
    return merged[cols]

print(ai_zone_area_report(rooms, zones))
slides.explainHead: Read it before the output loads
slides.explainBody: This function claims to reproduce the zone report from cells [1] and [5]. Read it line by line - two of these lines look correct but are not - before the next slide reveals what it actually printed.
slides.teaching: Give students this exact function. Have them predict, out loud, whether it will error - it will not; both bugs fail silently.

slides.title: [7] AI-audit, continued: what it actually printed
slides.output:
zone       area_m2  mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr
0  North  2.649809e-08                    NaN
1  South  2.649809e-08                    NaN
slides.explainHead: Two silent bugs, one broken table
slides.explainBody: Bug 1: .str.lower() makes the join key 'north'/'south', but zones_gdf still has 'North'/'South' - merge silently finds no matches, so mean_energy_kwh_m2_yr is NaN for every row. Bug 2: .geometry.area runs before any reprojection, so the column named area_m2 actually holds meaningless square-degree values. Neither line raises an error - both fail silently.
slides.teaching: Require students to name both defects before accepting this output. Same exact function and output as authored - split across two slides only so the full function fits the code panel at full size.

slides.title: Studio 5: diagnose and repair the AI-generated function
slides.prompt: Both bugs above run without any error message.
steps: Name the merge-key defect and where it was introduced.
Name the CRS defect and where it was introduced.
Rewrite the function fixing both.
Confirm your fixed version reproduces 239.74 m2 and the correct energy values.
slides.teaching: Require running the fixed function and comparing its output to cell [5]'s known-good numbers before accepting the repair.

slides.title: Every reprojected number from today, checked against ground truth
slides.callout: Same rule, three quantities: a geographic-CRS number is real math applied to the wrong unit; the projected column always lands within a fraction of a percent of a known truth.
slides.teaching: Have students say, for each row, which column they would trust and why - identical drill to 07A's summary table, now run on this studio's own numbers.

slides.title: The lightweight transfer safeguard, applied to a new metric

left.head: What changes
left.body: Same pipeline, a different spatial metric: perimeter length (zones_utm.geometry.length) instead of area, plus a second, previously-unused 8.0 m room pair (R102-R103) instead of R101-R102.

right.head: Why it counts as transfer
right.body: Length needs the same projected CRS as area - proving you understand the general rule, not just one memorized example. You write the assert statements yourself, against your own predicted values.

slides.teaching: State plainly that this satisfies the required weekly self-generated check - it is graded, not optional.

slides.title: [8] Self-check: perimeter, then prepare a second pair
slides.code:
zones_utm['perimeter_m'] = zones_utm.length
print(zones_utm[['zone', 'perimeter_m']])

coords = [(-76.134977, 43.039407),
          (-76.134879, 43.039407)]
pair = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {'room_id': ['R102', 'R103']},
    geometry=[Point(xy) for xy in coords], crs=4326)
slides.explainBody: The known 24 m × 10 m rectangle has a 68 m perimeter. The projected result (68.01 m) is close, not magically exact. The next slide measures the point pair.
slides.teaching: This transfer check changes the spatial metric from area to perimeter.

slides.title: [8] continued: measure the second pair in both CRSs
slides.code:
d_deg = pair.geometry.iloc[0].distance(pair.geometry.iloc[1])
pair_utm = pair.to_crs('EPSG:32618')
pts_utm = pair_utm.geometry
d_m = pts_utm.iloc[0].distance(pts_utm.iloc[1])
print(f'R102-R103 in EPSG:4326 (degrees): {d_deg:.6f}')
print(f'R102-R103 in EPSG:32618 (meters): {d_m:.3f}')
slides.explainBody: R102-R103, a different 8.0 m pair than Meeting A's demo, reproduces the identical 0.000098-degrees / 8.010-meters pattern - proof the rule generalizes, not a coincidence of one pair of rooms.
slides.teaching: This is the exact 'different row/case/parameter' the plan's transfer safeguard requires - name it as such to students.

slides.title: Studio 6: write your own boundary assertions
slides.prompt: Turn the two checks above into 2-4 self-written assert statements.
steps: Assert both zones' perimeter_m is within 0.1 m of the known 68.0 m.
Assert d_m is within 0.1 m of the known 8.0 m.
Assert d_deg is much smaller than 0.001 (still meaningless as meters).
Run from a restarted kernel and confirm silent success.
slides.teaching: Required, graded transfer-safeguard element - a script with all four assertions passing silently is the expected deliverable, not optional polish.

slides.title: One merge, one reprojection, one honest map
takeaways: Attribute data merges onto geometry exactly like any other pandas merge - by a shared key.
Always reproject to a justified projected CRS before computing area, length, or any distance.
239.74 m2 against a known 240 m2, and 68.01 m against a known 68 m, are both small, honest projection distortion - not errors.
A choropleth is a labeled Matplotlib figure like any other - color just encodes one more attribute.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students state their own Project 1 site's planned EPSG code and one sentence justifying it, tying directly into next week's compiled draft.
